verdict.rationale: Nix's own CLI provides per-project environments: `nix-shell` and `nix develop` build or download the declared dependencies and open a shell with the right environment. A flake can be built from the current directory, multiple versions of a package can coexist, and community users confirm teams rely on `nix-shell` for correct dependencies. The evidence never explicitly documents a version-controlled per-project file (e.g. shell.nix/flake.nix committed to the repo) as the source of truth, nor automatic switching when entering a project directory, so coverage is partial. missing for 10: explicit documentation of a checked-in per-project config file pinning runtime/tool versions, automatic per-directory environment switching, and hands-on corroboration of pinning specific language runtime versions.

support.subject: As a developer, I can install and switch language runtimes or tool versions per project from a checked-in config file

citations.quote: the command `nix-shell` will build or download those dependencies if they’re not already in your Nix store, and then start a Bash shell in which all necessary environment variables (such as compiler search paths) are set.
`nix develop` - run a bash shell that provides the build environment of a derivation
Nix makes it trivial to share development and build environments for your projects, regardless of what programming languages and tools you're using.

You can have multiple versions or variants of a package installed at the same time. This is especially important when different applications have dependencies on different versions of the same package
you can do `nix-shell --run "<some command>"`, and it will make sure you have all of the correct dependencies.
